Passover. Known in Hebrew as Pesach, this eight-day festival begins on the fifteenth of Nisan, falling in March or April. It commemorates the Exodus from Egypt and the liberation of the Israelites from slavery, centering on the eating of matzah, unleavened bread, and the retelling of the Exodus story with its themes of freedom, redemption, and divine providence.

The seder is a ceremonial meal featuring symbolic foods: bitter herbs, called maror; charoset, a sweet paste; an egg; a lamb shank; and matzah. Each represents aspects of the Exodus story. Matzah, eaten throughout the holiday, recalls the haste with which the Israelites left Egypt and had no time for bread to rise. The Haggadah is the text recited during the seder, telling the Passover story in prayers, blessings, and songs, with traditions varying across different Jewish communities.

Chametz, leavened products, is completely forbidden, and the week before Passover involves a thorough removal of all leavened foods from the home. Four cups of wine are drunk during the seder, representing the four expressions of redemption in the biblical narrative. The holiday is one of the three pilgrimage festivals in biblical tradition, when Jews would journey to the Temple in Jerusalem.

The plague of the firstborn is the final plague, after which Pharaoh releases the Israelites, and Passover commemorates both the plague and the salvation of Jewish firstborns. The holiday is deeply tied to concepts of freedom, making it a symbol of liberation movements and human dignity across cultures and centuries. It is rooted in the Exodus narrative found in the Book of Exodus and has become one of the most widely observed Jewish holidays, central to Jewish identity and practice.
